questions.q: Without Continuous Access Evaluation, how long is a standard Microsoft Entra ID access token normally honored by a resource provider once issued?
options: For its full signed lifetime, commonly around an hour, regardless of what happens to the account afterward
Only until the next Conditional Access policy refresh, typically a few seconds
Indefinitely, with no expiry of any kind
Only for the duration of the user's active mouse or keyboard input
questions.explain: Standard OAuth access tokens are honored for their full lifetime, commonly on the order of an hour, unless a mechanism like CAE intervenes to revoke them early.

questions.q: What problem does Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) solve?
options: It replaces the need for Conditional Access policies at sign-in
It closes the gap where an already-issued token keeps being honored even after a critical account event, by revoking access in near real time
It shortens every access token's lifetime to a few seconds by default
It eliminates the need for Microsoft Entra ID Protection risk scoring
questions.explain: CAE creates a near-real-time channel so resource providers can revoke access within minutes of a critical event, instead of waiting for the token to expire naturally.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed in this lesson as a CAE critical event?
options: A user opens a new browser tab
A device's compliance policy is updated with a new OS version requirement
An administrator explicitly revokes a user's refresh tokens
A user's manager changes in the org chart
questions.explain: The critical events CAE reacts to include account disable/delete, password change or reset, explicit admin revocation of refresh tokens, and a high user-risk evaluation from Identity Protection.

questions.q: How does the lesson distinguish a login-time Conditional Access check from Continuous Access Evaluation?
options: They are the same mechanism described with two different names
Login-time checks only apply to admin accounts, while CAE applies to all accounts
CAE replaces Conditional Access and makes login-time checks unnecessary
Login-time checks ask whether a request was trustworthy when made; CAE asks whether the session is still trustworthy right now
questions.explain: These answer different questions: Conditional Access evaluates trust at the moment of sign-in, while CAE re-evaluates trust continuously as new critical signals arrive during the session.

questions.q: With CAE in place, what changes about how a resource provider can treat token lifetime as a security lever?
options: A longer-lived token can be held with more confidence, because revocation depends on a pushed critical-event signal rather than the token's natural expiry
Token lifetime becomes irrelevant to security, since CAE disables all tokens after five minutes
Tokens must now be reissued every time a Conditional Access policy is edited
Shortening token lifetime becomes the only way to limit a compromise's damage window
questions.explain: Without CAE, shortening token lifetime is one of the few ways to limit damage after a compromise. With CAE, revocation no longer depends on expiry, so a longer-lived token is less risky to hold.
